CHAPTER XCIII

One day as he lay there sighing and groaning, prayerless, tuneless,
hopeless, a thought flashed into his mind. What he had done for the
poor and the wayfarer, he would do for himself. He would fill his den of
despair with the name of God and the magic words of holy writ, and the
pious, prayerful consolations of the Church.

Then, like Christian at Apollyon's feet, he reached his hand suddenly
out and caught, not his sword, for he had none, but peaceful labour's
humbler weapon, his chisel, and worked with it as if his soul depended
on his arm.

They say that Michael Angelo in the next generation used to carve
statues, not like our timid sculptors, by modelling the work in clay,
and then setting a mechanic to chisel it, but would seize the block,
conceive the image, and at once, with mallet and steel, make the marble
chips fly like mad about him, and the mass sprout into form. Even so
Clement drew no lines to guide his hand. He went to his memory for the
gracious words, and then dashed at his work and eagerly graved them in
the soft stone, between working and fighting.

He begged his visitors for candle ends, and rancid oil.

“Anything is good enough for me,” he said, “if 'twill but burn.” So at
night the cave glowed afar off like a blacksmith's forge, through the
window and the gaping chinks of the rude stone door, and the rustics
beholding crossed themselves and suspected deviltries, and within the
holy talismans, one after another, came upon the walls, and the sparks
and the chips flew day and night, night and day, as the soldier of
Solitude and of the Church plied, with sighs and groans, his bloodless
weapon, between working and fighting.

Kyrie Eleison.

Christe Eleison.

{ton Satanan suntripson upo tous pothas ymwn}(1)

Sursum Corda.(2)

Deus Refugium nostrum et virtus.(3)

Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi miserere mihi.(4)

Sancta Trinitas unus Deus, miserere nobis.(5)

Ab infestationibus Daemonum, a ventura ira, a damnatione perpetua.
Libera nos Domine.(6)

Deus, qui miro ordine Angelorum ministeria, etc, (the whole collect).(7)

Quem quaerimus adjutorem nisi te Domine qui pro peccatis nostris juste
irascaris? (8)

Sancte Deus, Sancte fortis, Sancte et misericors Salvator, amarae morti
ne tradas nos.

And underneath the great crucifix, which was fastened to the wall, he
graved this from Augustine:

O anima Christiana, respice vulnera patientis, sanguinem morientis,
pretium redemptionis. Haec quanta sint cogitate, et in statera mentis
vestrae appendite, ut totus vobis figatur in corde, qui pro vobis totus
fixus est in cruce. Nam si passio Christi ad memoriam revocetur, nihil
est tam durum quod non aequo animo toleretur.

Which may be thus rendered: O Christian soul, look on the wounds of
the suffering One, the blood of the dying One, the price paid for our
redemption! These things, oh, think how great they be, and weigh them in
the balance of thy mind: that He may be wholly nailed to thy heart,
who for thee was all nailed unto the cross. For do but call to mind the
sufferings of Christ, and there is nought on earth too hard to endure
with composure.

Soothed a little, a very little, by the sweet and pious words he was
raising all round him, and weighed down with watching and working night
and day, Clement one morning sank prostrate with fatigue, and a deep
sleep overpowered him for many hours. Awaking quietly, he heard a little
cheep; he opened his eyes, and lo! upon his breviary, which was on a low
stool near his feet, ruffling all his feathers with a single pull, and
smoothing them as suddenly, and cocking his bill this way and that with
a vast display of cunning purely imaginary, perched a robin redbreast.

Clement held his breath.

He half closed his eyes lest they should frighten the airy guest.

Down came robin on the floor.

When there he went through his pantomime of astuteness; and then,
pim, pim, pim, with three stiff little hops, like a ball of worsted on
vertical wires, he was on the hermit's bare foot. On this eminence he
swelled and contracted again, with ebb and flow of feathers; but Clement
lost this, for he quite closed his eyes and scarce drew his breath in
fear of frightening and losing his visitor. He was content to feel the
minute claw on his foot. He could but just feel it, and that by help of
knowing it was there.

Presently a little flirt with two little wings, and the feathered
busybody was on the breviary again.

Then Clement determined to try and feed this pretty little fidget
without frightening it away. But it was very difficult.

He had a piece of bread within reach, but how get at it? I think he was
five minutes creeping his hand up to that bread, and when there he must
not move his arm.

He slily got a crumb between a finger and thumb and shot it as boys do
marbles, keeping the hand quite still.

Cockrobin saw it fall near him, and did sagacity, but moved not.

When another followed, and then another, he popped down and caught up
one of the crumbs, but not quite understanding this mystery fled with
it, for more security, to an eminence; to wit, the hermit's knee.

And so the game proceeded till a much larger fragment than usual rolled
along.

Here was a prize. Cockrobin pounced on it, bore it aloft, and fled so
swiftly into the world with it, the cave resounded with the buffeted
air.

“Now, bless thee, sweet bird,” sighed the stricken solitary; “thy wings
are music, and thou a feathered ray camedst to light my darkened soul.”

And from that to his orisons, and then to his tools with a little bit of
courage, and this was his day's work:

     Veni, Creator Spiritus,
     Mentes tuorem visita,
     Imple superna gratia
     Quae tu creasti pectora

     Accende lumen sensibus,
     Mentes tuorum visita,
     Infirma nostri corporis,
     Virtute firmans perpeti.

And so the days rolled on; and the weather got colder, and Clement's
heart got warmer, and despondency was rolling away; and by-and-by,
somehow or another, it was gone. He had outlived it.

It had come like a cloud, and it went like one.

And presently all was reversed; his cell seemed illuminated with joy.
His work pleased him; his prayers were full of unction; his psalms of
praise. Hosts of little birds followed their crimson leader, and flying
from snow, and a parish full of Cains, made friends one after another
with Abel; fast friends. And one keen frosty night as he sang the
praises of God to his tuneful psaltery, and his hollow cave rang forth
the holy psalmody upon the night, as if that cave itself was Tubal's
surrounding shell, or David's harp, he heard a clear whine, not
unmelodious; it became louder and less in tune. He peeped through
the chinks of his rude door, and there sat a great red wolf moaning
melodiously with his nose high in the air.

Clement was rejoiced. “My sins are going,” he cried, “and the creatures
of God are owning me, one after another.” And in a burst of enthusiasm
he struck up the laud:

“Praise Him all ye creatures of His!

“Let everything that hath breath praise the Lord.”

And all the time he sang the wolf bayed at intervals.

But above all he seemed now to be drawing nearer to that celestial
intercourse which was the sign and the bliss of the true hermit; for he
had dreams about the saints and angels, so vivid, they were more like
visions. He saw bright figures clad in woven snow. They bent on him eyes
lovelier than those of the antelope's he had seen at Rome, and fanned
him with broad wings hued like the rainbow, and their gentle voices bade
him speed upon his course.

He had not long enjoyed this felicity when his dreams began to take
another and a strange complexion. He wandered with Fra Colonna over the
relics of antique nations, and the friar was lame and had a staff,
and this staff he waved over the mighty ruins, and were they Egyptian,
Greek, or Roman, straightway the temples and palaces, whose wrecks they
were, rose again like an exhalation, and were thronged with the famous
dead. Songsters that might have eclipsed both Apollo and his rival
poured forth their lays; women, god-like in form, and draped like
Minerva, swam round the marble courts in voluptuous but easy and
graceful dances. Here sculptors carved away amidst admiring pupils, and
forms of supernatural beauty grew out of Parian marble in a quarter of
an hour; and grave philosophers conversed on high and subtle matters,
with youth listening reverently; it was a long time ago. And still
beneath all this wonderful panorama a sort of suspicion or expectation
lurked in the dreamer's mind. “This is a prologue, a flourish, there is
something behind; something that means me no good, something mysterious,
awful.”

And one night that the wizard Colonna had transcended himself, he
pointed with his stick, and there was a swallowing up of many great
ancient cities, and the pair stood on a vast sandy plain with a huge
crimson sun sinking to rest, There were great palm-trees; and there
were bulrush hives, scarce a man's height, dotted all about to the sandy
horizon, and the crimson sun.

“These are the anchorites of the Theban desert,” said Colonna calmly;
“followers not of Christ and His apostles, and the great fathers, but
of the Greek pupils of the Egyptian pupils of the Brachmans and
Gymnosophists.”

And Clement thought that he burned to go and embrace the holy men and
tell them his troubles, and seek their advice. But he was tied by the
feet somehow, and could not move, and the crimson sun sank, and it got
dusk, and the hives scarce visible, And Colonna's figure became shadowy
and shapeless, but his eyes glowed ten times brighter; and this thing
all eyes spoke and said: “Nay, let them be, a pack of fools I see how
dismal it all is.” Then with a sudden sprightliness, “But I hear one of
them has a manuscript of Petronius, on papyrus; I go to buy it; farewell
for ever, for ever, for ever.”

And it was pitch dark, and a light came at Clement's back like a gentle
stroke, a glorious roseate light. It warmed as well as brightened. It
loosened his feet from the ground; he turned round, and there, her face
irradiated with sunshine, and her hair glittering like the gloriola of a
saint, was Margaret Brandt.

She blushed and smiled and cast a look of ineffable tenderness on him,
“Gerard,” she murmured, “be whose thou wilt by day, but at night be
mine!”

Even as she spoke, the agitation of seeing her so suddenly awakened him,
and he found himself lying trembling from head to foot.

That radiant figure and mellow voice seemed to have struck his nightly
keynote.

Awake he could pray, and praise, and worship God; he was master of his
thoughts. But if he closed his eyes in sleep, Margaret, or Satan in her
shape, beset him, a seeming angel of light. He might dream of a thousand
different things, wide as the poles asunder, ere he woke the imperial
figure was sure to come and extinguish all the rest in a moment, stellas
exortus uti aetherius sol; for she came glowing with two beauties never
before united, an angel's radiance and a woman's blushes.

Angels cannot blush. So he knew it was a fiend.

He was alarmed, but not so much surprised as at the demon's last
artifice. From Anthony to Nicholas of the Rock scarce hermit that had
not been thus beset; sometimes with gay voluptuous visions, sometimes
with lovely phantoms, warm, tangible, and womanly without, demons
within, nor always baffled even by the saints. Witness that “angel form
with a devil's heart” that came hanging its lovely head, like a bruised
flower, to St. Macarius, with a feigned tale, and wept, and wept, and
wept, and beguiled him first of his tears and then of half his virtue.

But with the examples of Satanic power and craft had come down copious
records of the hermits' triumphs and the weapons by which they had
conquered.

Domandum est Corpus; the body must be tamed; this had been their
watchword for twelve hundred years. It was a tremendous war-cry; for
they called the earthly affections, as well as appetites, body, and
crushed the whole heart through the suffering and mortified flesh.

Clement then said to himself that the great enemy of man had retired
but to spring with more effect, and had allowed him a few days of
true purity and joy only to put him off his guard against the soft
blandishments he was pouring over the soul that had survived the
buffeting of his black wings. He applied himself to tame the body, he
shortened his sleep, lengthened his prayers, and increased his severe
temperance to abstinence. Hitherto, following the ordinary rule, he had
eaten only at sunset. Now he ate but once in forty-eight hours, drinking
a little water every day.

On this the visions became more distinct.

Then he flew to a famous antidote, to “the grand febrifuge” of
anchorites--cold water.

He found the deepest part of the stream that ran by his cell; it rose
not far off at a holy well; and clearing the bottom of the large stones,
made a hole where he could stand in water to the chin, and fortified by
so many examples, he sprang from his rude bed upon the next diabolical
assault, and entered the icy water.

It made him gasp and almost shriek with the cold. It froze his marrow.
“I shall die,” he cried, “I shall die; but better this than fire
eternal.”

And the next day he was so stiff in all his joints he could not move,
and he seemed one great ache. And even in sleep he felt that his very
bones were like so many raging teeth, till the phantom he dreaded came
and gave one pitying smile, and all the pain was gone.

Then, feeling that to go into the icy water again, enfeebled by fasts
as he was, might perhaps carry the guilt of suicide, he scourged himself
till the blood ran, and so lay down smarting. And when exhaustion began
to blunt the smart down to a throb, that moment the present was away,
and the past came smiling back. He sat with Margaret at the duke's
feast, the minstrels played divinely, and the purple fountains gushed.
Youth and love reigned in each heart, and perfumed the very air.

Then the scene shifted, and they stood at the altar together man and
wife. And no interruption this time, and they wandered hand in hand, and
told each other their horrible dreams. As for him, “he had dreamed she
was dead, and he was a monk; and really the dream had been so vivid and
so full of particulars that only his eyesight could even now convince
him it was only a dream, and they were really one.”

And this new keynote once struck, every tune ran upon it. Awake he
was Clement the hermit, risen from unearthly visions of the night, as
dangerous as they were sweet; asleep he was Gerard Eliassoen, the happy
husband of the loveliest and best, and truest girl in Holland: all the
happier that he had been for some time the sport of hideous dreams, in
which he had lost her.

His constant fasts, coupled with other austerities, and the deep mental
anxiety of a man fighting with a supernatural foe, had now reduced
him nearly to a skeleton; but still on those aching bones hung flesh
unsubdued, and quivering with an earthly passion; so, however, he
thought; “or why had ill spirits such power over him?” His opinion was
confirmed, when one day he detected himself sinking to sleep actually
with a feeling of complacency, because now Margaret would come and he
should feel no more pain, and the unreal would be real, and the real
unreal, for an hour.

On this he rose hastily with a cry of dismay, and stripping to the skin
climbed up to the brambles above his cave, and flung himself on them,
and rolled on them writhing with the pain: then he came into his den a
mass of gore, and lay moaning for hours; till, out of sheer exhaustion,
he fell into a deep and dreamless sleep.

He awoke to bodily pain, and mental exultation; he had broken the fatal
spell. Yes, it was broken; another and another day passed, and her image
molested him no more. But he caught himself sighing at his victory.

The birds got tamer and tamer, they perched upon his hand. Two of them
let him gild their little claws. Eating but once in two days he had more
to give them.

His tranquility was not to last long.

A woman's voice came in from the outside, told him his own story in a
very few words, and asked him to tell her where Gerard was to be found.

He was so astounded he could only say, with an instinct of self-defence,
“Pray for the soul of Gerard the son of Eli!” meaning that he was dead
to the world. And he sat wondering.

When the woman was gone, he determined, after an inward battle, to risk
being seen, and he peeped after her to see who it could be; but he took
so many precautions, and she ran so quickly back to her friend, that the
road was clear.

“Satan!” said he directly.

And that night back came his visions of earthly love and happiness so
vividly, he could count every auburn hair in Margaret's head, and see
the pupils of her eyes.

Then he began to despair, and said, “I must leave this country; here I
am bound fast in memory's chain;” and began to dread his cell. He said,
“A breath from hell hath infected it, and robbed even these holy words
of their virtue.” And unconsciously imitating St. Jerome, a victim
of earthly hallucinations, as overpowering, and coarser, he took his
warmest covering out into the wood hard by, and there flung down under
a tree that torn and wrinkled leather bag of bones, which a little ago
might have served a sculptor for Apollo.

Whether the fever of his imagination intermitted, as a master mind of
our day has shown that all things intermit(9) or that this really broke
some subtle link, I know not, but his sleep was dreamless.

He awoke nearly frozen, but warm with joy within.

“I shall yet be a true hermit, Dei gratia,” said he.

The next day some good soul left on his little platform a new lambs-wool
pelisse and cape, warm, soft, and ample.

He had a moment's misgiving on account of its delicious softness and
warmth; but that passed. It was the right skin(10), and a mark that
Heaven approved his present course.

It restored warmth to his bones after he came in from his short rest.

And now, at one moment he saw victory before him if he could but live
to it; at another, he said to himself, “'Tis but another lull; be on thy
guard, Clement.”

And this thought agitated his nerves and kept him in continual awe.

He was like a soldier within the enemy's lines.

One night, a beautiful clear frosty night, he came back to his cell,
after a short rest. The stars were wonderful. Heaven seemed a thousand
times larger as well as brighter than earth, and to look with a thousand
eyes instead of one.

“Oh, wonderful,” he cried, “that there should be men who do crimes by
night; and others scarce less mad, who live for this little world, and
not for that great and glorious one, which nightly, to all eyes not
blinded by custom, reveals its glowing glories. Thank God I am a
hermit.”

And in this mood he came to his cell door.

He paused at it; it was closed.

“Why, methought I left it open,” said he, “The wind. There is not a
breath of wind. What means this?”

He stood with his hand upon the rugged door. He looked through one of
the great chinks, for it was much smaller in places than the aperture
it pretended to close, and saw his little oil wick burning just where he
had left it.

“How is it with me,” he sighed, “when I start and tremble at nothing?
Either I did shut it, or the fiend hath shut it after me to disturb my
happy soul. Retro Sathanas!”

And he entered his cave rapidly, and began with somewhat nervous
expedition to light one of his largest tapers. While he was lighting it,
there was a soft sigh in the cave.

He started and dropped the candle just as it was lighting, and it went
out.

He stooped for it hurriedly and lighted it, listening intently.

When it was lighted he shaded it with his hand from behind, and threw
the faint light all round the cell.

In the farthest corner the outline of the wall seemed broken.

He took a step towards the place with his heart beating.

The candle at the same time getting brighter, he saw it was the figure
of a woman.

Another step with his knees knocking together.

IT WAS MARGARET BRANDT.

     (1) Beat down Satan under our feet.

     (2) Up, hearts!

     (3) O God our refuge and strength.

     (4) O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world,
     have mercy upon me!

     (5) O Holy Trinity, one God, have mercy upon us.

     (6) From the assaults of demons--from the wrath to come--
     from everlasting damnation, deliver us, O Lord!

     (7) See the English collect, St., Michael and all Angels.

     (8) Of whom may we seek succour but of Thee, O Lord, who for
     our sins art justly displeased (and that torrent of prayer,
     the following verse).

     (9) Dr. Dickson, author of Fallacies of the Faculty, etc.

     (10) It is related of a mediaeval hermit, that being offered
     a garment made of cats' skins, he rejected it, saying, “I
     have heard of a lamb of God but I never heard of a cat of
     God.”

One day—after many such days—he lay upon his rude pallet and let the groans go out of him as if they were his only breath. No prayer rose with them, no psalm kept time, no hope leaned on them. The cave was a mouth of black stone that seemed to swallow all sound and give back only his own misery, thickened and made dull.

Then, sudden as a spark struck from flint, a thought came clean through the smoke of his mind: what he had done for the poor and the wayfarer, he would do for himself. He had fed other men’s bodies to keep their souls from fainting; he would feed his own soul to keep it from dying.

He reached, not for a sword—he had none—but for the humbler iron that honest labour wields: his chisel. His hand closed on it as if on a handle of life. He set its edge against the soft stone of his wall and began to work with a fury that was half craft and half combat. He drew no guiding lines; he did not pause to measure; he went straight to memory, to the storehouse of words that had once been the common bread of his days, and he drove them into the stone as if engraving them could nail them inside his heart.

He begged from any who came near—shepherds, women with baskets, children shy as hares—for candle-ends and rancid oil. “Anything is good enough for me,” he would say, with the plain humility of a man who has ceased to bargain with comfort, “if ’twill but burn.” By night the little cell shone through its window and the gaping seams of the door like a smithy at work; and the rustics, hearing the steady chip and seeing that unnatural glow, crossed themselves and whispered of devilry. Yet within, the only magic was the old Church’s spell of syllables, cut into rock with aching wrists while the body starved and the mind wrestled.

Kyrie Eleison. Christe Eleison. Sursum Corda. Deus Refugium nostrum et virtus. Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere mihi. Sancta Trinitas unus Deus, miserere nobis. Ab infestationibus Daemonum, a ventura ira, a damnatione perpetua. Libera nos Domine. And the long collect—Deus, qui miro ordine Angelorum ministeria—spilled from his recollection as naturally as water from a jar once filled.

Beneath the great crucifix, fixed against the stone like a judgment and a refuge, he graved Augustine’s counsel, word by word, as one sets loaves in an oven, trusting the heat will do what hands cannot: O anima Christiana, respice vulnera patientis… Look, Christian soul, on the wounds, on the blood, on the price; weigh it in the balance of the mind until He is nailed to the heart who for thee was nailed to the cross—so that, remembering Christ’s Passion, nothing on earth remains too hard to bear with a level spirit.

The sweet sentences, set up about him like a fence against darkness, soothed him—little, very little—but the labour and watching ground him down. One morning, his limbs gave way as if the bones had been unpegged; he fell full length and sleep poured over him, deep and heavy, for hours.

When he woke, it was quietly; the first thing that met him was not fear, but a small sound, a thin cheep, like a needle of music pricking through wool. He opened his eyes.

Upon his breviary, laid on a low stool near his feet, perched a robin redbreast. The bird fluffed its feathers with one brisk pull, smoothed them with the next, cocked its head this way and that in an elaborate pretence of slyness, and looked as if it had invented caution and was proud of it.

Clement held his breath. He narrowed his eyes lest even the shine of them should startle this bright scrap of life away. The robin dropped to the floor and performed its little comedy of craft, then—pim, pim, pim—hopped in three stiff jerks like a ball of worsted dancing on wires, and landed upon the hermit’s bare foot.

He shut his eyes altogether then; he was content to feel, scarcely feel, the minute claw—feel it only because he knew it was there. After a moment the busybody flicked its wings and was back upon the breviary.

Clement, who had fed many mouths in better days and knew how gentleness must be measured, resolved to offer this guest a crumb without frightening it. A piece of bread lay within reach. To reach it was a whole task: he crept his hand towards it inch by inch until his fingers touched the crust, and then he dared not move his arm. He pinched a morsel and shot it with thumb and finger as boys shoot marbles, keeping his hand as still as a stone.

The robin saw it fall near, did its pantomime of sagacity, and would not move. Another crumb followed, then another. At last the bird darted down, snatched one, and, not trusting the mystery, fled with it to a safer height—namely, the hermit’s knee. So the game went on, a quiet traffic between hunger and trust, until a larger fragment than usual rolled out and lay like a prize.

The robin pounced, lifted it, and fled so swiftly into the world that the cave rang with the beat of buffeted air.

“Now bless thee, sweet bird,” sighed the stricken solitary. “Thy wings are music, and thou, a feathered ray, camedst to light my darkened soul.”

The sound of that flight—so small, so certain—tuned him like a string. He turned back to his orisons and then to his tools with a morsel of courage, and this was the day’s carving:

Veni, Creator Spiritus,
Mentes tuorum visita,
Imple superna gratia
Quae tu creasti pectora…
and so onward, the prayer shaped like a chant, the chant like a hearth-fire’s steady breathing.

Thus the days rolled. The weather sharpened; the cold came with clear teeth. Yet, strangely, Clement’s heart warmed. Despondency, that had come upon him like a cloud that blots out all landmarks, began to thin. It had not been argued away; it was outlived. One morning he perceived it was gone, as a man notices the fever is broken because the room looks itself again.

Then all was reversed. The cell that had been a den seemed lit from within. His work pleased him; his prayers had unction; his psalms became praise instead of pleading. Birds—hosts of them—followed their crimson leader and, fleeing the snow and a parish full of Cains, made friends one by one with Abel, and then fast friends. The cave’s soundscape, once mere echo and groan, filled with the scratch of claws on stone, with quick chirrs and feather-rustlings—small domestic noises that were as homely as a pot simmering in a poor cottage, and as wholesome.

One keen frosty night, as he sang to his psaltery, the hollow cave flung back the holy psalmody upon the dark as if the stone itself were a great instrument’s shell. Then he heard, outside, a long clear whine—not unmelodious. It rose and fell, grew louder and less in tune. He peeped through the chinks of his rude door and saw a great red wolf sitting and moaning with its nose high in the air, as though the sky were a bowl and it drank the cold.

Clement’s heart leaped. “My sins are going,” he cried, “and the creatures of God are owning me, one after another.” In a burst of fervour he struck up: “Praise Him, all ye creatures of His! Let everything that hath breath praise the Lord.” And at intervals, between his lines, the wolf bayed—answering, it seemed, in the only liturgy it knew.

After this, he believed himself drawing nearer to that celestial intercourse which saints had promised and hermits sought. His dreams grew vivid, not like common dreams, but like visions. Bright figures, clad in woven snow, leaned over him; eyes lovelier than any antelope’s he had once seen at Rome looked down; broad wings hued like a rainbow fanned him; gentle voices bade him speed and endure. Sleep, which had been an abyss, became a chapel.

But he had not long enjoyed this felicity when the dreams changed, and their taste went strange.

He wandered again with Fra Colonna among the relics of antique nations. The friar was lame now and leaned upon a staff; and when he waved that staff over ruins—Egyptian, Greek, or Roman—temples and palaces rose at once from their wrecks like breath from warmed glass, complete and crowded with the famous dead. The air filled with music: songsters who seemed to eclipse Apollo himself poured out their lays; women, godlike and draped like Minerva, moved in voluptuous yet effortless dances through marble courts. Sculptors carved while pupils watched; and forms of supernatural beauty sprang from Parian marble in the time it takes to knead a loaf and set it near the coals. Philosophers, grave and subtle, conversed while youth listened reverently. It was like a whole world restored—and still, underneath that splendour, an unease lay coiled in Clement’s mind.

This is a prologue, he thought. There is something behind. Something that means me no good.

One night, when the wizard Colonna surpassed himself, he pointed with his stick, and many great ancient cities were swallowed up. They stood upon a vast sandy plain beneath a huge crimson sun sinking toward rest. Palm-trees stood in black shapes; and everywhere on the sand were low bulrush hives, scarcely a man’s height, dotted to the horizon.

“These are the anchorites of the Theban desert,” said Colonna calmly—“followers not of Christ and His apostles and the great fathers, but of the Greek pupils of the Egyptian pupils of the Brachmans and Gymnosophists.”

Clement burned to run and embrace those lonely men, to tell them his trouble and ask their counsel. Yet he found his feet held fast, tied by something he could not see. The crimson sun sank; dusk thickened; the hives faded. Colonna’s figure grew shadowy and shapeless, but his eyes shone tenfold brighter; and that thing—all eyes—spoke: “Nay, let them be. A pack of fools; I see how dismal it all is.”

Then, with sudden sprightliness: “But I hear one of them has a manuscript of Petronius, on papyrus. I go to buy it. Farewell for ever—for ever—for ever.”

It became pitch dark; and behind Clement there came a light, gentle as a hand laid warm upon the shoulder—a glorious roseate light that both brightened and heated. It loosened his feet. He turned.

There stood Margaret Brandt, her face irradiated with sunshine, her hair glittering like a saint’s gloriola. She blushed and smiled, and her look was tenderness itself, unbearable in its truth.

“Gerard,” she murmured, “be whose thou wilt by day, but at night be mine.”

The very shock of her presence awakened him. He lay trembling from head to foot, as if the dream had struck a tuning-fork in his nerves and left it humming.

Awake, he could pray, praise, and worship; he could marshal his thoughts and drive them where he willed. But let him close his eyes, and Margaret—or Satan wearing her likeness—came to beset him, a seeming angel of light. He might dream a thousand things, as wide apart as poles, yet before waking her image would blaze and extinguish all else in a moment, as the sun makes lesser stars vanish. She came with two beauties never joined in heaven: an angel’s radiance and a woman’s blush. Angels cannot blush; therefore he knew it was a fiend.

The discovery alarmed him; yet it did not astonish him as much as the artifice’s fineness. From Anthony to Nicholas of the Rock, what hermit had not been thus assaulted? Sometimes by gross voluptuousness, sometimes by tender phantoms warm and womanly without and demoniac within. The records of such wars were part of his meat and drink. With those records came also the victories, and the weapons.

Domandum est Corpus. The body must be tamed. For twelve hundred years that cry had rung through the caves and deserts. They had called even the heart’s earthly affections “body,” and crushed it through mortified flesh. Clement told himself the enemy had only withdrawn to strike more surely; had given him days of purity and joy to lull him, and now poured soft blandishments over the soul that had stood the buffeting of black wings.

So he set himself to tame the body. He shortened sleep, lengthened prayer, and pressed temperance into abstinence. Hitherto he had eaten only at sunset; now he ate but once in forty-eight hours, and drank a little water daily.

The visions grew more distinct.

Then he flew to the anchorites’ famous antidote, their grand febrifuge: cold water. A stream ran by his cell, rising not far away at a holy well. He found its deepest reach and cleared the bottom of stones, making a hole where he could stand with water to his chin. Fortified by the examples he had read till they seemed like family lore, he sprang from his rude bed upon the next diabolical assault and plunged in.

The icy water stole his breath. It made him gasp, almost shriek; it froze his marrow. “I shall die,” he cried through chattering teeth, “I shall die; but better this than fire eternal.”

Next day he was so stiff he could scarcely move. Every joint seemed a hinge ground with sand; he was one ache from crown to heel. Even in sleep he felt his bones like so many raging teeth—until the phantom he dreaded came, gave one pitying smile, and all pain was gone, as if her presence were a balm.

Then, fearing that to go again into the icy stream—enfeebled by fasting as he was—might carry the guilt of suicide, he scourged himself till blood ran; and he lay down smarting. When exhaustion dulled the sting to a throbbing, the present slipped away and the past came smiling back.

He sat with Margaret at the duke’s feast; minstrels played so divinely that their notes seemed to gild the air; purple fountains gushed. Youth and love reigned in every heart and perfumed the very breath. Then the scene shifted, and they stood at the altar together, man and wife. No interruption came this time. They wandered hand in hand, and told each other their horrible dreams. He confessed he had dreamed she was dead and he a monk—and the dream had been so vivid, so crowded with particulars, that only his waking sight could now persuade him it had been false, and that they were truly one.

Once that keynote was struck, every tune ran upon it. Awake he was Clement the hermit, risen from visions as dangerous as they were sweet; asleep he was Gerard Eliassoen, happy husband of the loveliest, best, and truest girl in Holland—happier still for having lately been tormented by hideous dreams in which he had lost her.

Austerity had reduced him nearly to a skeleton; yet still, on those aching bones, flesh seemed unsubdued, quivering with earthly passion—or why should ill spirits have such power? His fear was confirmed when one day he caught himself sinking toward sleep with a shameful complacency, because now Margaret would come and he should feel no more pain; the unreal would be real, and the real unreal, for an hour.

He sprang up with a cry of dismay. Stripping to the skin, he climbed to the brambles above his cave and flung himself upon them, rolling and writhing. The thorns bit like hooked knives. He came back a mass of gore and lay moaning for hours, until sheer exhaustion dropped him into deep, dreamless sleep.

He woke to bodily pain and mental exultation. He had broken the fatal spell. Another day passed, then another; her image molested him no more.

Yet he caught himself sighing at his victory.

The birds grew tamer and tamer. They perched upon his hand. Two of them even let him gild their little claws, holding still with the solemn patience of creatures that live by light and seed and do not invent torment. Eating but once in two days, he had more crumbs to give them; and the soft scratch of their feet on his palm was like a small domestic comfort, the way a familiar ladle’s tap against a pot can steady a weary mind.

His tranquillity did not last.

A woman’s voice came from outside and, in a very few words, told him his own story—told it as if it were already a tale traded in the market—and asked him where Gerard was to be found. The sound struck him harder than a blow, because it carried the world’s language into his hermitage and named him in the tongue of men.

So astonished was he that instinct, not reason, answered. “Pray for the soul of Gerard the son of Eli,” he said—meaning that Gerard was dead to the world. Then he sat, staring at stone, while his heart thumped like a mallet on wood.

When the woman was gone, he fought an inward battle and determined to risk being seen; he peeped out after her to discover who she could be. But he took so many precautions, and she ran so quickly back to her friend, that when at last he dared look, the road was empty and harmless as if no human voice had ever travelled it.

“Satan!” said he directly.

That night the visions returned with a vengeance. Earthly love and happiness flooded him so vividly he could count every auburn hair on Margaret’s head, see the very pupils of her eyes as though she were before him in daylight. Despair rose again, and with it a new fear of his own cell.

“I must leave this country,” he whispered. “Here I am bound fast in memory’s chain.” And then, with sudden loathing: “A breath from hell hath infected it, and robbed even these holy words of their virtue.”

Unconsciously imitating Jerome in his own warfare with hallucinations, he took his warmest covering out into the wood hard by and flung himself under a tree—torn, wrinkled, a leather bag of bones that not long ago might have served a sculptor for Apollo. Whether his imagination’s fever intermitted—since all things, they say, intermit—or whether the change of place broke some subtle link, he did not know; but his sleep was dreamless.

He woke nearly frozen, yet warm with joy within. “I shall yet be a true hermit, Dei gratia,” he said.

Next day some good soul left on his little platform a new lamb’s-wool pelisse and cape, warm, soft, ample. For a moment he misgave at its delicious softness—so like an invitation to the body. Then the scruple passed. It was the right skin, a token that Heaven approved his present course. When he came in from his short rest, it put warmth back into his bones as broth restores a fainting man: not luxurious, but sustaining.

Now he would see victory before him if he could but live to it; then again he would tell himself, trembling, “’Tis but another lull. Be on thy guard, Clement.” The thought kept his nerves in continual awe. He lived like a soldier within the enemy’s lines, listening to every sound as if sound itself might betray him.

One night—a beautiful, clear, frosty night—he returned to his cell after a short rest in the wood. The stars were wonderful. Heaven seemed a thousand times larger, and brighter too, than earth; and to look with a thousand eyes instead of one.

“Oh, wonderful,” he cried, “that there should be men who do crimes by night; and others scarce less mad, who live for this little world, and not for that great and glorious one, which nightly—if custom have not blinded—reveals its glowing glories. Thank God I am a hermit.”

In this mood he came to the door of his cave and paused. It was closed.

“Why, methought I left it open,” said he. “The wind? There is not a breath of wind. What means this?”

He laid his hand on the rugged door. Through one great chink—since the door in places was far smaller than the hole it pretended to stop—he saw his little oil wick burning exactly where he had left it.

“How is it with me,” he sighed, “when I start and tremble at nothing? Either I did shut it, or the fiend hath shut it after me to disturb my happy soul. Retro Sathanas!”

He entered rapidly and set about, with nervous haste, to light one of his largest tapers. As he kindled it, a soft sigh sounded within the cave.

He started and dropped the candle at the very instant it caught; it went out. He stooped, seized it, and lighted it again, listening so hard he seemed to listen with his skin. When it burned, he shaded it with his hand and threw the small light about the cell.

In the farthest corner the outline of the wall was broken.

He took a step toward it, his heart beating. Another step—his knees knocking together.

It was the figure of a woman.

IT WAS MARGARET BRANDT.
